The Nādabindu Upaniṣad.
Peace: "May my speech be established in my mind... The nature of the Vairāja Praṇava.
The syllable *a* is known as the right wing, while *u* is remembered as the left;
they say that *m* is the tail, and the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) is the head.
His feet and other limbs are his qualities; his body is said to be the ultimate reality (tattva).
Dharma is his right eye, and that which is known as adharma is the other.
The Bhūrloka is at his feet, while the Bhuvarloka is at his knees;
the Suvarloka is in the region of his hips, and the Maharloka is in the region of his navel.
The Janaloka is in the region of the heart; the Tapasloka is in the throat;
and the Satyaloka is situated between the eyebrows and the middle of the forehead.
I worship that state which the yogi attains after burning away the three types of karma by the fire of knowledge born from the meditation on the Self as Vairāja.
Indeed, this Nādabindu Upaniṣad, which is a division of the Ṛgveda,
first reveals the Virāṭ-Praṇava and then describes the attainment of the qualified Brahman by those who know that qualified Brahman, in accordance with their own realized knowledge.
Having first revealed the true nature of Brahman as devoid of distinctions,

[this work] unfolds, manifesting the liberation-in-the-body (*vikalebara-kaivalya*)— which arises from the power of destroying the three types of karma— for those who are endowed with the means of practice for the knowledge of that [Brahman].
It [the Great Vairāja Praṇava] manifests itself in its intermediate form. A commentary on this, based on a brief text, is now commenced.

Regarding the *ṛti*—beginning with the letter "A" and so forth—the Mahāvairāja-praṇava is said to consist of twelve mātrās, formed by unifying the internal Virāṭ and the Praṇava. For the sake of attaining that state, [this concerns] the Mahāvirāja.

This is the statement regarding the nature of the Suparṇa. This letter *A*, which denotes the gross phenomenal world (*sthūla-prapañca*), is the right wing of the Great Virāj who has attained the state of Suparṇa.
Its left wing, however, is traditionally held to be the letter *U*, which denotes the subtle phenomenal world (*sūkṣma-prapañca*). Of that...
The knowers of Brahman say that the letter *ma* is the tail, which expresses the proliferation (*prapañca*) of seeds;

they declare that the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*), however, has become its head. Its feet and so forth are the qualities of *sattva* and the rest. Its body, moreover, is endowed with distinguished limbs.

The collection of ninety-six principles (*tattva*) mentioned in the Vārāhopaniṣad is now described. His right and left eyes are *dharma* and *adharma*; [the word] "right eye" involves a change of gender [*liṅgavyatyaya*]. In his feet, knees, hips, navel, heart, throat, and between the eyebrows are the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr.
The meaning is "established. "Of the feet" is the locative dual. || 3-4 ||
The fruit of the Vairāja-vidyā is this mantra, which exceeds a thousand syllables, as it has been demonstrated here;
thus, one who is skilled in the application of the breath (saṃhayaoga) should mount upon this [mantra]. || 5 ||
It is not broken even by hundreds of millions of sinful acts.
He says "sahasra" to indicate that the Vairāja-praṇava is distinguished by such specific qualities;
[the phrase] "sahasrārṇam" involves a change of gender (from neuter to masculine). This refers to the form of the first part of the praṇava.

It is heard in scripture that it possesses a thousand parts: "The letter *A* is endowed with a thousand parts. Here, within this Great King Praṇava, this mantra *Oṃ* is endowed with the letter *A* characterized by the part known as the thousand syllables.
The phrase "abides as the denoter" means that it is revealed by the Vedic scriptures. The word "vā" (or) is used for emphasis.
Thus, I am the Great Virāj, the meaning of the Praṇava consisting of the twelve mātrās which is about to be described.
Such continuous contemplation is *haṃsayoga*. To explain that for one who possesses this there is non-difference from [the Self] despite the presence of sin and so forth, he says "evam" (thus).

Because one destroys (*hanti*) all mental constructions (*kalanā*) other than one's own true nature through the knowledge of that true nature, one is called *haṃsa*. The continuous contemplation that "I am indeed He" is *haṃsayoga*. One who is proficient in that is [the practitioner].

The yogin who knows that [is as follows]: || 5 || When one has ascended to the Great Vairāja-vidyā characterized in the manner described above and becomes intent upon its contemplation, then one is never at any time divided by even hundreds of millions of sins arising from karma, produced by the movements of one's own performed actions— thus [it is said].
He shows the fruit of the knowledge that is about to be described.
Regarding the nature of the four primary measures (mātrās) of the Praṇava:
the first measure belongs to Agni, and the next one likewise belongs to Vāyu.
The subsequent mātrā should be like the orb of the sun;
the supreme half-mātrā, which the wise know as Vāruṇī, [is the next].
In which these measures are firmly established throughout the three periods of time—this is declared to be the syllable Om; understand it through the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās).

He describes the nature of the fourfold measure of Pradhāna: "The fiery one," etc. Agni is Vaiśvānara; that which is related to him is the "fiery" (āgneyī) first measure, known by the name Vairājyakārā. Likewise, by the word "Vāyu," the Sūtrātman is expressed, for it is said, "O Gautama, Vāyu [is indeed Brahman]."

Because of the scriptural statement, "That is the thread," this second measure, which belongs to that [thread], is the supreme *vāyavī* (etheric) form of the syllable *ukāra*. It shines perfectly like the orb of the sun; thus, being the essence of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), it is "resembling the solar orb" (*bhānumaṇḍalasaṃkāśa*). Its designation is the nature of the syllable *akāra*.
The supreme third *mātrā* is like the orb of the sun;
furthermore, O wise ones, that which is the half-*mātrā* (*ardhamātrā*)— being the highest and most excellent in relation to the three *mātrās*—
is so called because it wards off (or rather, pervades) the entire multitude of distinctions imagined by oneself through its own nature.
Varuṇa is the fourth; they know her as Vāruṇī, who possesses his form and consists of the fourth mātrā.
In that *praṇava*, these measures (*mātrās*) are established throughout the three periods of time beginning with the past;

this is how the *oṃkāra* is described by the Śrutis. O people who lack self-knowledge, you [should contemplate] the *mātrās* beginning with *Ghoṣiṇī*, which consist of the five *ghaṭikās* of time to be described hereafter.
"By means of the dhāraṇās, understand"—that is to say, "know. || 8 ||
p. 217) An exposition on the twelve-fold division of the *praṇava*’s measures (*mātrā*), consisting of both individual and collective aspects:
The first measure is Ghoṣiṇī; likewise, the next is Vidyunmātrā.
Pataṅginī shall be the third, and the fourth is Vāyuveginī. (9)
The fifth is indeed named Nāmadheyā, while the sixth is called Aindrī;
the seventh is named Vaiṣṇavī, and the eighth is Śāṅkarī.
The ninth is named Mahatī; Dhṛti is considered the tenth;
the eleventh shall be Nārī; and the supreme Brāhmī is the twelfth.
He explains the twelvefold division consisting of both individual and collective measures with the verse beginning "Ghoṣiṇī."
9 || The internal *mātrās* of the *praṇava*, beginning with the letter *a*, should be known as denoting the five *brahmans*. 10 ||
The letters beginning with 'A', as the collective whole, become the designators of the cosmic egg, Virāṭ, and so forth. || 11 ||
Regarding the fruit of the departure [of life] at each respective measure for lay followers:
"But if one is separated from the vital breaths during the first measure, he is born as a sovereign emperor, the king of the land of Bharata. (12)
One who has departed [from life] on the second day becomes a high-souled yakṣa;
on the third, a vidyādhara; and on the fourth, a gandharva.
Furthermore, if one is separated from the vital breaths during the fifth measure,
having dwelt together with the deities, he is glorified in the world of Soma.
In the sixth [century], one attains union with Indra; in the seventh, the station of Viṣṇu;
and in the eighth, one goes to Rudra, the Lord of Creatures.
On the ninth day, however, one goes to Maharloka; on the tenth, to Jana;
on the eleventh, to Tapoloka; and on the twelfth, to the eternal Brahman.
Having thus established the visualization for twelve *mātrās* within the sixty *ghaṭikās*,
he describes the fruit of the departure [of the breath] at the time of each respective *mātrā* for one who performs the worship, beginning with the words "In the first":
the five *ghaṭikās* beginning with the arising of the form named Ghoṣiṇī, which has the four-faced Brahmā as its presiding deity.

If a lay practitioner (upāsaka) should thus depart from his life-breaths during the first measure, which is limited by time, that yogi is reborn as a sovereign king (sārvabhauma) over the land of Bhārata. And likewise in the second [measure]; the dative case is used here in the sense of the locative.
The eleventh sequence should be inferred in the same manner as the first sequence. || 13-16 ||
The nature of Brahman is without distinction; and the fruit of the knowledge of that is even beyond it—pure, all-pervading, stainless, and auspicious.
The supreme Brahman is eternally manifest, from which the rising of all lights proceeds. (17)
When the mind, which transcends the senses and is beyond all qualities, becomes absorbed,
the one engaged in yoga shall always enter that incomparable, auspicious, and peaceful state.
A living being joined with that [practice] and absorbed in it, having abandoned all attachments through the practice of yoga, may gradually leave behind his long-standing lineage. || 19 ||
Then, his bonds dissolved, that stainless lord of Kamalā experiences supreme bliss through that very state of Brahman.
Having thus described the gradation of fruits for those who know Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa-brahma*),

he states the nature of Brahman without attributes (*nirviśeṣa-brahma*) and the fruit of that knowledge, beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*). "Then"— that is, from the passage beginning "The letter *A* is the right wing," up to the point where Brahman with attributes is designated as the Great Vairāja.
The worshipers of that [state] and its fruit have been described; beyond that is what is established through the negation (*apahnava*) of the portions to be abandoned within the Great Vairāja state.
For this very reason, it is pure, even though from the perspective of those lacking self-knowledge (*svājñadṛṣṭi*), there is the possibility of the impure *aśiva* pervading it.

It is all-pervasive, stainless, and auspicious; that from which the rising of the lights such as the sun occurs—this is Brahman, eternally risen. When the mind, which animates the collection of instruments (the senses) and their cause—the three qualities—is dissolved, having transcended the senses, gone beyond the qualities, and become devoid of attributes, then [one attains that state]. || 17 ||

That which remains as Brahman— ever incomparable, peerless, auspicious because it is pure consciousness alone, and tranquil as that which transcends all else— one who is engaged in non-conceptual yoga (*nirvikalpaka-yoga*) should enter into that. When a living being is united with that yoga, having become one with That, he enters his own causal family (*kula*), which consists of the effects of his own dualistic ignorance.

One should release [the breath] very slowly; then that which remains for a long time is pure consciousness (cinmātra). To the question, "Who is the one qualified in this way?", he says: "well-established" (saṃsthita). This means being perfectly established through the practice of yoga (yogābhyāsa).
To the question, "How can there be a desire for the practice of yoga in one who is attached to internal and external mental constructs? he says:

"Free from all attachments" (19). Therefore, the yogi, having become pure within and having dissolved the bonds of his own fetters—the snares that are extraneous to himself—becomes a lord (*prabhu*) by virtue of the lotus of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*). He is the one who, through that very [state] which has been realized by himself, [attains] supreme bliss.

Through the yoga of knowledge, one realizes that Brahman—which is established by the total negation of everything through the state of being Brahman—is one's own non-dual self alone; the meaning is that one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 20 ||
The Knower’s Reflection on the Existence or Non-existence of Prārabdha-karma:
"O high-minded one, having known the Self constantly, pass your time; experiencing all that has been set in motion by past karma (prārabdha), you ought not to feel agitation. (21)
Once self-knowledge has arisen, one does not abandon the prārabdha at all;
however, after the dawning of the knowledge of reality, the prārabdha no longer exists.
But because the body and so forth do not exist [for one who has awakened], it is like a dream upon waking;
that which is called "commenced" (prārabdha) karma is that which belongs to another birth. (23)
Since there is no other birth for the person at any time, this very body is indeed superimposed just like the body in a dream. (24)

(220) From what could that which is superimposed have birth? In the absence of birth, from what could there be persistence? One perceives the material cause of the phenomenal world to be like that of an earthen vessel. 25.

And ignorance is [the cause] according to the Vedāntas; when that is destroyed, where is there any "universality" (viśvatā)? Just as one might grasp a snake out of delusion while abandoning the rope. (26)
In the same way, one of deluded intellect perceives the world without realizing its true nature;
once the rope is fully recognized, the form of the snake no longer remains. || 27 ||

When the substratum is thus known and the phenomenal world has become emptiness, since the body too is part of that phenomenon, how can there be any persistence of *prārabdha* (the momentum of past karma)? || 28 ||
It is said that this has been undertaken for the purpose of awakening ignorant people;
thereafter, when the *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion) has reached its exhaustion solely through the power of time, [liberation occurs]. (29)
The sound resulting from the union of the Brahman and the Praṇava, which is Śiva consisting of light—
that Self manifests of its own accord, like the sun when the clouds have vanished.
Addressing one whose knowledge is yet immature, he says this: "The Self," and so forth.

Having known one's own Self as Brahman through the constant practice of hearing and other means obtained by the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, O high-minded one, spend the remainder of your life.

While experiencing all that has been set in motion by *prārabdha*—whether pleasure or pain arising from desire, aversion, or the desire of another, or their mixture—you ought not to feel agitation or distress. Even when such self-knowledge has arisen within you, *prārabdha* does not release you; if [it remains] for you...

Then, indeed, the knowledge of the reality that is Brahman alone arises; he says "tattvajñāna" (knowledge of reality) [in verse 22] to indicate that for you there is no longer any *prārabdha* karma. He states the reason for the possibility of *prārabdha* in the words "dehādīnām" (of the body, etc.): that karma belonging to another birth which bestows the experience of pleasure and so forth.
That *prārabdha* (the momentum of past actions) indeed perishes through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), like a dream upon awakening;

the reason for this is that, in reality, the body and other such things do not exist. Thus, since there is no further birth for the person once the body and so forth are non-existent, that which you consider to be *prārabdha*—
The meaning is that one should resolve that [the body] never exists at any time.
He clarifies the non-existence of the body, which remains dependent on *prārabdha* (past karma), by means of an illustration: "In a dream... (verses 24–25).

One's own ignorance (*svājñāna*) is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). When that [ignorance] has reached the state of non-existence through the Vedāntas—by means of knowledge (*jñāna*), realization (*vijñāna*), and perfect wisdom (*samyagjñāna*)—how can its effect, the universe (*viśvatā*), possibly persist? For everything from the body up to the universe is included within it [the universe]. It cannot.
The meaning is that at some point the triad of karmas, beginning with *prārabdha*, exists. The remainder is clear.

(26–28) If this is so, how can there be the conceptualization of *prārabdha*? To this he says: "By ignorance," etc. [The question is: once one's own ignorance and its effects have been destroyed by one's own knowledge, how can that body exist?

The meaning is that this conceptualization of "prārabdha" (commenced karma) is intended to restrain speech by implying compliance with one's own ignorance. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From that.
That is, subsequent to perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), by the power of time and solely through the grace of the Lord (*īśvara*).
When the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself— characterized by the persistence of *prārabdha* karma— has reached its end through negation (*apahnava*),

then the awakening born from the prior contemplation of the Brahman-Pranava no longer yields the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself; for Śiva, who is composed of light, is the Nāda of the Turyātīta state.
Having been like the sun when the clouds have departed, the Self manifests by itself;
the meaning is that only the Self remains. || 30 ||

The yogi, seated in the Siddhāsana and maintaining the Vaiṣṇavī Mudrā, should constantly listen to the internal sound (nāda) within the right ear; this contemplation of sound is the means for attaining the fourth state of the fourth.
This sound, when practiced, veils external noise;
having conquered all opposing factors within two fortnights, one shall attain the state of the Fourth (turya).
It is heard that at the first stage of practice, various kinds of great sounds are heard;
likewise, as one progresses in practice, they are heard to become increasingly subtle.
In the beginning, it arises like the ocean, clouds, kettledrums, and waterfalls;
in the middle, it has the sound of a mṛdaṅga drum, as well as that of bells and trumpets.
But at the end, there are the sounds of tinkling bells, flutes, lutes, and bees;
thus various kinds of sounds are heard, becoming increasingly subtle. (35)
But when the loud sound of great kettledrums and other instruments is being heard,
one should there contemplate only the subtle, even more subtle resonance.
Whether the mind is delighting in the gross while abandoning the subtle, or in the subtle while abandoning the gross,
one should not cause it to wander elsewhere.
Wherever the mind first settles upon a sound, having become steady there, it dissolves along with that sound. (38)
Having forgotten all external objects, the mind—like milk and water—becomes one with the *nāda* and then suddenly dissolves into the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). (39)
Then, becoming indifferent and always self-restrained through practice,
one should immediately focus one's attention solely upon the *nāda* that brings about the state of *unmanī*.
Having completely abandoned all thought and being devoid of all physical activity, one should focus exclusively on the sound (nāda); in that sound, the mind dissolves.

He describes the method of contemplating the *nāda* (the subtle sound) as a means for attaining the *turyātīta* (the state beyond the fourth), which is the meaning of the *brahmapraṇava*: "By means of the *siddhāsana*," and so forth.
Pressing the anus with the left [foot] and the right [foot] above the genitals, with the body straightened by the three bindings— this becomes Siddhāsana.

Thus, the yogin established in the siddhāsana well-known in the Yogaśāstra, with the internal object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from blinking or opening the eyes—this is that Vaiṣṇavī mudrā, hidden in all the tantras. (p. 223)

Thus, having contemplated the Vaiṣṇava mudrā established by the Śruti, one should always hear the internal sound (nāda) located in the anāhata-cakra through the right ear. To the question, "What results from hearing the sound in this way?", he says: "When practiced," and so forth; thus the sound is practiced.

Having enveloped the external sounds and other objects that veil his own [nature], and having eradicated the existence of anything other than himself— which constitutes his own opposite— by means of the mere *pakṣa* (the internal state), the yogi who employs *nāda* as his means shall proceed to the state of *turyātīta* (the fourth beyond the fourth) as being his own self alone. [He realizes] the full extent of *nāda*.
And he reveals the experience resulting from that practice: "It is heard" (verse 33). How? "At first" (verses 34–35).

To the question, "What is that which is to be grasped?", he says: "Great" (verse 36). He says, "Dense" (verse 37), meaning that one should not cause [the mind] to waver from the sound in any way whatsoever. Among the sounds ranging from those of the ocean and so forth up to the humming of bees, in whichever—

He says [in the verses] beginning with "where" (yatra) that the mind becomes steady where, and through that sound, it dissolves into the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). [Verse 38–39]. Indifferent toward other activities [verse 40]. Since the practice of sound (nādābhyāsa) yields fruit quickly, for that very reason, [one should abandon] all thought [verse 41].
Just as a bee drinking nectar does not heed other fragrances, so the mind, when constantly attached to the sound (nāda),
does not desire sense objects. 42.
Bound by the fragrance of the beautiful sound, the mind immediately abandons its restlessness; through the grasping of that sound, the serpent residing within the inner organ is subdued.
Forgetting everything, the mind—like a wild elephant roaming through the garden of sense-objects—runs distractedly toward some single point. (44)
This sound, capable of leading [beings] to certainty, is a sharp goad; this resonance acts as a snare for binding the deer of the inner self. (45)

And even when the inner wave is obstructed, it acts like the shore; he states, with an illustration, that the mind attached to the *nāda* does not desire any object beyond it: "The honey... (verse 42). [The mind] is bound by the noose of *nāda* and the suspension of breath.

He says "bound" (baddha) because the mind, being motionless, forgets both its own external and internal [objects] and becomes rigid. The meaning is that, having forgotten its own internal and external [objects], it remains steady in itself and does not run about anywhere. He says "mind" (manaḥ), [implying] that the hook of sound (nādāṅkuśa) is skillful in restraining the elephant of the mind.
The expert [teacher] says that *nāda* is like a net on the shore that obstructs the waves of the birds within the inner self—thus he says:
"Nāda" (verse 45).
The nature of the sound to be attained is the resonance joined with the Brahman-Pranava, consisting of the essence of light. || 46 ||
The mind dissolves therein; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The conceptualization of space persists only as long as sound continues to proceed. (47)
That which is soundless is proclaimed as the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self;
as long as there is sound, so long is there mind, but at the end of sound is Manonmanī.

When the syllable has ceased, there is sound with resonance; when the syllable is exhausted, there is the soundless supreme state. Through constant contemplation upon the resonance (nāda), latent impressions (vāsanā) become completely exhausted.
The mind and the vital breath dissolve into the stainless state, without a doubt;
so too do thousands of millions of *nādas* and hundreds of millions of *bindus*. (50)
All dissolve there into the sound of the *brahmapraṇava*.

(p. 225) Having explained the nature of the means (*upāya*) through the *nāda*, he now reveals the nature of the goal (*upeya*) consisting of the fruit, as well as the fruit of that knowledge—beginning with the word "Brahman. [It is] differentiated from the gross portion of the letter *A* and so forth.

Because it nourishes the conceptualization of the states beginning with waking-waking and ending with the single flavor of permission (anujñaikarasa), Brahman shines within that *praṇava* which consists of sixteen measures; that is the *brahmapraṇava*. Being attached to that and non-different from it, it is the "Nada" (Sound), so called because it does not grant an outward-facing state (*parāgbhāva*) to those who know it. That very thing is [the Nada].
The resonance (nāda) is the inner self (pratyagātman); by virtue of its self-luminosity, it consists of light. || 46 ||

That mind which is the cause of the distinction between the external and the internal dissolves into that Supreme Brahman which is non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman). That which is the substratum of the state of one's own ignorance, as indicated by the mind—that belongs to Viṣṇu;
[the word] "tad-viṣṇoḥ" refers to Him whose nature is to pervade in dependence upon that which is to be pervaded.
When the state of being a pervader dependent on a pervaded ceases to exist, that which remains— devoid of even the conceptualization of the pervaded and the pervader— is the supreme, non-dual,
and undifferentiated; it is called "pada" (the ground) because one attains (*padyate*) it as being nothing other than That alone.

The meaning is "isolation within the physical body" (*vikalebarakaivalya*). He states the limit [of practice] by asking: "Should one always perform the contemplation of the Brahman-Praṇava?"—namely, with the words "as long as. As long as there is the perception of external and internal sounds, desires, and so forth, so long does the mental construction of space—the phenomenal world of sound and the rest, which is considered separate from oneself—exist [or not exist].

It becomes free from the conceptualization of delusion. (47) Therefore, it is correctly said that "this Supreme Self shines forth through silence. He states the limit of the contemplation of the *nāda* and its fruit, beginning with the word "nāda" (48–49). He describes how the *nāda* of the Brahman-praṇava serves as the substratum for the sublation of everything else:

All those thousands of millions of means that exist as methods for attaining Nāda, the witness of all; and those hundreds of millions of means for attaining Bindu, the Lord, which result in the attainment of states such as Sālokya—[all] those [are surpassed by this]. 50.

By virtue of the word "ca" (and), whatever modifications there may be imagined by those ignorant of their own Self, they all go to dissolution therein— in that Brahman which is the sound of the Praṇava, non-different from the inner Self. Consequently, Brahman, which is non-different from the inner Self, being without anything to be presided over, becomes without a substratum.
The sense is that only its own self remains.
For yogis who have ascended the nāda, there is the attainment of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), which is free from all states and devoid of all thought. || 51 ||
He remains as if dead; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt. He never hears the sound of conchs or drums.
In the state of Unmanī, the body is certainly known to be like a piece of wood;
it perceives neither cold nor heat, nor likewise pain or pleasure. (53)
Having completely abandoned both pride and humiliation through meditative absorption, the mind of the yogi never again pursues the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. (54)
Freed from both waking and sleep, one should attain the state of one's own true nature.
He whose vision is steady without an object to behold,
whose breath is steady without effort,
and whose mind is steady without a support— [he is liberated].
He is the form of the resonance within the interval between the Brahma-star. || 56 ||
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.

Thus, he clarifies the state of yogins who have ascended to the sound of the *brahmapraṇava* and their fulfillment of their duties with the verse beginning "All" (vv. 51–52). Having attained the state of being solely Brahman, the yogin does not perceive any conceptualization apart from Brahman, nor [anything] other than Brahman.
The meaning is that [the Self] consists of the nature of both existence and non-existence, being devoid of any counterpart (niṣpratiyogika).
(Verses 53–55) Showing that this [Self] has the form of the resonance of the *brahmapraṇava*, he concludes with the word "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*):
"Of whom the vision, breath, and mind, having become steady without the conceptualization of the object, effort, or support..."

They culminate in Brahman and the Praṇava. This wise one remains as the nature of Nāda, designated as the Turya-turya within the Tāraka-Brahman; the meaning is that he becomes liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta). Thus end the words of the Upaniṣad.
These two [words] signify the conclusion of the Nādabindu Upaniṣad.

This concise and lucid commentary on the *Nādabindu* has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra. This commentary on the *Nādabindu* consists of one hundred and fifty [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Nādabindūpaniṣad, completing the thirty-eighth [treatise] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
